title: How to get a contractor license in Minnesota (step by step)
dek: Minnesota has no "general contractor license." Here's which license you actually need, what's on the exam, and the deadlines that cost contractors money.
text:
You're good at the work. Homeowners keep asking if you can take the whole job. But the second you look up how to get licensed in Minnesota, you land on a state website full of forms, codes and statute numbers. 
 I help run a family framing and contracting business here in Minnesota, so I've been through this maze. Here's the plain-words version. 
 First: Minnesota doesn't have a "general contractor license" 
 This trips up almost everyone. What Minnesota has is a  residential building contractor license , issued by the Department of Labor and Industry (DLI). There are also two smaller versions: 
   License  What it lets you do  
  Residential building contractor (BC)  Everything, including new homes and detached garages  
  Residential remodeler (CR)  Work on existing homes only  
  Residential roofer (RR)  Roofing only (not gutters, soffit or fascia)   
 Commercial work is different. It's handled by local cities, not the state. 
 Do you even need a license? 
 Generally, yes, if you contract  directly with a homeowner  on a home with one to four units, and the job covers  more than one skill area  (say, framing plus drywall plus trim). 
 If you only work as a sub for a licensed contractor, you usually don't need your own license. There's also an exemption for very small operations. Check DLI's certificate of exemption to see if you qualify. 
 Why it matters: doing unlicensed work when you need a license is a misdemeanor in Minnesota, and cities can't issue you a building permit without one. 
 The 10 steps to getting licensed 
 
  Pick your business structure and name.  In Minnesota, the  business  gets licensed, not you personally. 
  File with the state and get your tax numbers.  
  Choose your qualifying person,  the owner or manager who takes the exam for the business. 
  Pass the exam.  More on this below. 
  Get insured.  General liability of at least $100,000 per occurrence and $300,000 total for bodily injury, plus $25,000 for property damage (or a $300,000 single-limit policy). 
  Apply for the license  through DLI. 
  Write bids and contracts that follow Minnesota law.  Everything in writing, including change orders. 
  Protect your pay with lien notices.  
  Hire subs and employees the right way,  including workers' comp. 
  Renew and keep up your continuing education:  14 hours every two-year license period. 
 
 What's on the Minnesota contractor exam? 
 
  110 multiple-choice questions  
  5.5 hours  to finish, and  70%  to pass 
 About  60% building code , and the rest on Minnesota laws and rules 
 No experience or school required to sit for it 
 
 They hand you the code book and a reference manual during the test. But 110 questions in 5.5 hours is about 3 minutes each. If you have to hunt for every answer, you'll run out of time. The people who pass know the most-tested numbers cold and know which chapter holds everything else. 
 If you fail, you wait  30 days  and submit a new application and fee. 
 The deadline that costs contractors the most money 
 It's the  pre-lien notice.  If you contract directly with a homeowner, the notice has to be in your written contract. With no written contract, you deliver it separately within  10 days  after the work is agreed on. Miss it, and you can lose your lien rights. 
 If a client won't pay, you generally have  120 days  after your last day of work to record a lien. 
 I keep a full step-by-step playbook with an exam study guide on my  Gumroad page  if you want everything in one place. 
 General information, not legal advice. Rules change, so confirm with the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry before you apply. Checked November 2026.  Contractor license Minnesota Exam

title: How to start a house cleaning business during school hours
dek: Price your first job and book clients around school pickup.
text:
You don't need a free week to start a cleaning business. You need the hours between school drop-off and pickup, one honest price, and a first client who tells a friend. 
 Start with the schedule you actually have. If drop-off is 8:00 and pickup is 3:00, your work window is about 8:30 to 2:30 once you count driving. That's one bigger clean or two small ones a day, and that's enough to start. Quote from that real window, not from the day you wish you had. 
 Price the first job without guessing 
 Walk the house once, count the rooms that get cleaned every visit, and time yourself honestly on your own house first. A simple worked example: 
 
  A 3-bedroom, 2-bath home, cleaned every two weeks  
 Your timed pace says about 2.5 hours, inside the school window. 
 Quoted flat at $145: a number you can say out loud without flinching. 
 
 The tool I build my bids with lives on my  Gumroad page , linked from the icons at the top of this site. 
 Book the second client before the first clean 
 Ask the first client one question at booking: "Who on your street hates cleaning?" One name is worth more than any ad. Send that person one short text the same day, while your name is still fresh.  Cleaning business School hours Pricing
